80415.e: Beetroot contains a strong red dye. Hands and clothes quickly turn red from it too.

80416.e: Turmeric is a yellow powder made from a root. It colours curries yellow, for example.

80417.q: In which water does a drop of food colouring spread faster?
80417.e: In warm water the tiniest particles move faster. That is why the colour spreads more quickly there.
80417.m: Colour spreads faster in warm water than in cold.

80418.q: What happens to a white flower that stands in water with food colouring for a few days?
a: The flower loses all its leaves
The flower grows twice as big
80418.e: The flower sucks the coloured water up through its stem. This way the colour reaches the flower head.
80418.m: A flower sucks water up through its stem to the flower head.

80419.q: Which vegetable provides a green colouring for food?
80419.e: Spinach contains a lot of green leaf pigment. You can use spinach to colour pasta green, for example.

80420.q: Which letter do the numbers of colourings on packaging start with?
80420.e: Additives such as colourings have an E number on packaging. Colourings have the numbers E 100 to E 199.
80420.m: Colourings are listed on packaging with an E number.

80421.q: You want to separate the colours of a felt-tip pen with water. Which paper do you put the dot of colour on?
80421.e: Coffee filter paper soaks up water well. The water can travel upwards in it and carry the colours with it.
80421.m: To separate colours, you need paper that soaks up water well.

80422.q: A coffee filter with a felt-tip dot stands in water. What travels up the paper and takes the colour with it?
80422.e: The paper soaks water up from the glass. The water dissolves the colour and carries it along.
80422.m: The water carries the colours up the paper.

80423.q: You draw a dot with a black felt-tip pen on a coffee filter and stand it in water. What do you soon see?
a: No colour at all any more
80423.e: Black felt-tip ink is often mixed from several colours. On the paper they separate, for example into blue, yellow and red.
80423.m: Black ink is often mixed from several colours.

80424.q: Where must the dot of colour be on the paper strip when it goes into the water?
80424.e: If the dot is in the water, the colour simply dissolves in the glass. If it is just above, the water rises up to it.
80424.m: The dot of colour must be just above the water.

80425.q: Which pens can you use to separate colours in paper with water?
80425.e: The colour must dissolve in water, otherwise it just stays put. That is why washable felt-tip pens work best.
80425.m: To separate colours with water, you need washable felt-tip pens.

80426.q: What does the Greek word ‘chroma’ in chromatography mean?
80426.e: ‘Chroma’ is the Greek word for colour. So chromatography means roughly ‘colour writing’.

80427.q: A coffee filter with a felt-tip dot stands in water. Why do different stripes of colour appear?
80427.e: Some colours are easily carried along by the water, others tend to stay behind. So they get different distances and separate.
80427.m: Each colour travels a different distance in the paper.

80428.q: Which pigments can you separate from green leaves with chromatography?
80428.e: Green leaves contain not only green but also yellow pigment. With methylated spirits instead of water, and with the help of an adult, you can separate them.
80428.m: Green leaves also contain yellow pigment.

80429.q: What can you use to make a simple invisible ink?
80429.e: Lemon juice is almost colourless and hard to see once dry. That is why it works well as invisible ink.
80429.m: Lemon juice is a simple invisible ink.

80430.q: How do you make writing in lemon juice visible again?
80430.e: When the paper is carefully warmed, for example with an iron, the dried juice changes colour. Only do this with an adult.
80430.m: Heat makes secret writing in lemon juice visible.

80431.q: What colour does lemon juice writing turn when heated?
80431.e: The juice contains sugar and other substances. When heated they turn brown, a bit like toast.

80432.q: Which drink from the fridge can also be an invisible ink?
80432.e: Dried milk is hard to see on white paper. When carefully warmed it turns brown and the writing appears.
80432.m: Milk can also be used as invisible ink.

80433.q: You write with a white candle on white paper. How do you make the writing visible?
80433.e: Wax repels water. The watercolour stays on the paper but not on the wax letters, so they show up light.
80433.m: Wax repels watercolour, so candle writing appears.

80434.q: What is the best thing to write on paper with lemon juice?
80434.e: You dip a cotton bud or a fine brush into the lemon juice and write with it. A pen would leave visible lines.
80434.m: Secret writing in lemon juice is done with a cotton bud or brush.

80435.q: You write with bicarbonate of soda water and then brush red cabbage juice over it. What happens?
80435.e: The bicarbonate of soda changes the colour of the red cabbage juice. That is why the letters appear in a different colour from the rest of the paper.
80435.m: Red cabbage juice can make bicarbonate of soda writing visible.

80436.q: What did people use invisible ink for in the past?
80436.e: With invisible ink, messages could be hidden. Only those who knew how to make it visible could read them.
80436.m: Invisible ink hides messages from prying eyes.

80437.e: Soap is made by boiling fats or oils with an alkali. This boiling is called soap making.
80437.m: Soap is made from fat and alkali.

80438.q: Why do you wash your hands with soap instead of just water?
80438.e: Water alone is poor at rinsing away greasy dirt. Soap wraps up the grease so that the water can rinse it away.
80438.m: Soap helps water rinse away greasy dirt.

80439.q: You sprinkle pepper on water and dip in a finger covered in soap. What does the pepper do?
80439.e: The soap weakens the stretched skin on the surface of the water. The water pulls back towards the edge and takes the pepper with it.
80439.m: Soap weakens the skin on the water.

80440.q: What were the craftsmen who used to make soap called?
80440.e: Soap was boiled in large pots. That is why the craftsmen were called soap boilers.
80440.m: In the past, soap boilers boiled soap in large pots.

80441.q: What forms when you rub soap with a little water between your hands?
80441.e: Soap and water form lots of tiny bubbles when rubbed. You know this white lather from washing your hands.

80442.q: When should you wash your hands with soap especially well?
a: After the toilet and before eating
80442.e: After using the toilet and before eating, clean hands are especially important. That way fewer germs get into your mouth.
80442.m: Wash your hands with soap after the toilet and before eating.

80443.q: A little paper boat has a drop of soap at the back. What happens in the water?
80443.e: The soap weakens the skin on the water at the back. At the front the water pulls more strongly, so the boat moves forwards.
80443.m: A drop of soap can power a paper boat.

80444.q: What happens to a bar of soap that lies in a puddle of water for a long time?
80444.e: Water slowly dissolves the soap at its surface. That is why it is better to let soap dry after washing.
80444.m: Soap in water goes soft and slimy.

80445.q: What is a simple, unscented bar of soap that is also used to wash clothes called?
80445.e: Household soap is a simple, solid soap. It is used, for example, to wash stains out of clothes.
80445.m: Household soap is a simple solid soap.

80446.q: What shape is a soap bubble that floats freely through the air?
80446.e: The thin soap skin pulls itself together as small as possible. The shape with the smallest surface is the sphere.
80446.m: A freely floating soap bubble is perfectly round.

80447.q: What is inside a soap bubble?
80447.e: When you blow, you blow air into the soap skin. Only the thin skin is made of soapy water.
80447.m: A soap bubble is full of air.

80448.q: Why does a soap bubble shimmer in many colours?
a: Light is reflected in the thin skin
80448.e: Light is reflected from the front and back of the thin soap skin. This creates shimmering rainbow colours.
80448.m: The thin skin of a soap bubble makes rainbow colours.

80449.q: What do you add to soapy water so that soap bubbles last longer?
80449.e: Glycerine is a thick, clear liquid. It stops the soap skin from drying out so quickly.
80449.m: Glycerine makes soap bubbles last longer.

80450.q: Why does a soap bubble burst after a while?
80450.e: The water in the soap skin evaporates and flows downwards. When the skin gets too thin, the bubble bursts.
80450.m: A soap bubble bursts when its skin gets too thin.

80451.q: What often happens if you carefully poke a soap bubble with a wet, soapy finger?
80451.e: A dry finger makes the bubble burst. But a finger with soapy water joins up with the soap skin.
80451.m: You can touch a soap bubble with a wet, soapy finger.

80452.q: What can happen to a soap bubble in very cold weather?
80452.e: In hard frost, the water in the soap skin freezes. Then you can see delicate ice patterns on the bubble.
80452.m: In hard frost, soap bubbles can freeze.

80453.q: About how thick is the skin of a soap bubble?
80453.e: The skin of a soap bubble is wafer-thin. It is much thinner than a human hair.
80453.m: The skin of a soap bubble is wafer-thin.

80454.q: What do you mix to make a simple bubble mixture?
80454.e: For soap bubbles you need water and something soapy such as washing-up liquid. Together they make a stretchy skin.
80454.m: Water and washing-up liquid make a bubble mixture.

80455.e: Foam is made of lots of bubbles full of air. Between the bubbles are thin walls of liquid.
80455.m: Foam is made of lots of little air bubbles.

80456.q: Which foam do you get when you beat egg white hard?
80456.e: When beating, air is stirred into the egg white. It turns white and stiff and is then called whisked egg white.
80456.m: Beaten egg white is called whisked egg white.

80457.q: What do you whip to make whipped cream?
80457.e: When whipping, air gets into the cream. The fat in the cream holds the bubbles in place.
80457.m: Whipping cream turns it into whipped cream.

80458.q: What do firefighters often use to put out burning petrol?
80458.e: The foam lies over the burning petrol like a blanket. Then no more air can reach the fire.

a: It contains a lot of flour
80459.e: Each bubble reflects a little light in all directions. Together the many bubbles look white, much like snow.
80459.m: Lots of little bubbles make foam look white.

80460.q: Where can you find solid foam?
80460.e: Foam rubber is solid foam with lots of air bubbles. That is why a mattress is soft and light.
80460.m: Foam rubber is solid foam full of air.

80461.q: Which drink often has a layer of milk froth on top?
80461.e: For a cappuccino, milk is frothed up with hot steam. The froth goes on top of the coffee.
80461.m: A cappuccino has milk froth on top.

80462.q: What happens to foam if you wait a long time?
80462.e: The thin walls of the bubbles get thinner over time and burst. That is why foam slowly sinks down.

80463.q: Why do you put washing-up liquid in the washing-up water?
a: It loosens the grease from the dishes
80463.e: Grease sticks to dishes and is hard to wash off with water alone. Washing-up liquid loosens the grease so the water can rinse it away.
80463.m: Washing-up liquid loosens grease from dishes.

80464.q: What happens if you add a little washing-up liquid to milk with drops of colour?
80464.e: The washing-up liquid changes the surface of the milk and loosens the milk fat. This sets the colours moving.
80464.m: Washing-up liquid sets drops of colour on milk moving.

80465.q: Why must ordinary washing-up liquid not go into the dishwasher?
a: It makes far too much foam
80465.e: Washing-up liquid foams a lot. In the machine the foam would pour out, so it needs its own product.
80465.m: Only dishwasher detergent goes into the dishwasher.

80466.q: You drip water onto a coin. What changes if there is washing-up liquid in the water?
a: Many more drops fit on it
80466.e: Pure water forms a high dome on the coin. Washing-up liquid weakens the skin of the water, so it overflows sooner.
80466.m: With washing-up liquid, water does not form such a high dome.

80467.q: What must you never do with washing-up liquid?
80467.e: Washing-up liquid is for cleaning, not for eating or drinking. Keep it where small children cannot reach it.

80468.q: How much washing-up liquid do you need for a bowl of washing-up water?
80468.e: Washing-up liquid works even in small amounts. Too much is unnecessary and pollutes the waste water.
80468.m: A few squirts of washing-up liquid are enough for the washing-up.

80469.q: Why should you put cream on your hands after a long time washing up?
a: Washing-up liquid dries out the skin
Washing-up liquid makes the skin hot
Washing-up liquid makes the skin thick
80469.e: Washing-up liquid removes not only grease from dishes but also the skin's natural oils. A cream gives the skin back its oils.
80469.m: Washing-up liquid can dry out the skin.

80471.q: What happens when you shake a bottle of oil and water hard?
80471.e: When shaken, the oil breaks up into lots of tiny droplets that float in the water. The liquid then looks cloudy.
80471.m: When shaken, oil in water breaks up into tiny droplets.

80472.q: What must you never use to put out burning oil in a pan?
80472.e: Water sinks under the hot oil, turns to steam at once and throws burning oil out. It is better to smother the fire with a lid.
80472.m: Never put out burning oil with water.

80473.q: Which sauce is made from oil and egg yolk that mix well?
80473.e: Egg yolk contains a substance that joins oil and water. That is why oil and egg yolk become a thick mayonnaise.
80473.m: Mayonnaise is a mixture of oil and egg yolk.

80474.q: In which drink are tiny droplets of fat spread through water?
80474.e: Milk is mostly water. Tiny droplets of fat float in it, which is why it is white and not see-through.
80474.m: Tiny droplets of fat float in milk.

80475.q: What do you call a mixture of tiny oil droplets in water?
80475.e: An emulsion is a mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix. One floats in tiny droplets in the other.
80475.m: A mixture of oil droplets in water is called an emulsion.

80476.q: What helps oil and water mix better?
80476.e: Washing-up liquid can cling to oil and to water at the same time. In this way it joins the two liquids.
80476.m: Washing-up liquid helps oil and water mix.

80477.q: Why can't you wash an oil stain out of a jumper with water alone?
a: Oil is too cold for it
80477.e: Water simply runs off the oil in beads. You need soap or detergent to loosen the oil.
80477.m: Wash oil stains with soap, not just with water.

80478.q: What do you do with a salad dressing of oil and vinegar just before serving?
80478.e: Oil and vinegar separate when the dressing stands. Shaking or stirring mixes them again.
80478.m: Shake a salad dressing well before serving.

80479.q: What makes the lumps of wax in a lava lamp rise?
80479.e: At the bottom of the lava lamp is a light bulb. It warms the wax, which expands, gets lighter and rises.
80479.m: In a lava lamp, heat makes the wax rise.

80480.q: What happens to the wax at the top of a lava lamp?
80480.e: It is cooler at the top than at the bottom. The wax cools, becomes heavier again and sinks back down.
80480.m: Cooled wax sinks down in a lava lamp.

80481.q: What do you see in a lava lamp?
a: Coloured blobs floating up and down
80481.e: In a lava lamp, soft, coloured blobs of wax float slowly upwards and back down again.
80481.m: In a lava lamp, blobs of wax float up and down.

80482.q: What makes the bubbles rise in a home-made lava lamp of water and oil?
80482.e: The effervescent tablet fizzes in the water and forms gas bubbles. These carry coloured drops of water upwards.
80482.m: An effervescent tablet makes a home-made lava lamp bubble.

80483.q: What does the food colouring colour in a home-made lava lamp of water and oil?
80483.e: Food colouring dissolves in water but not in oil. That is why the oil stays clear and only the water becomes coloured.
80483.m: Food colouring colours water but not oil.

80484.q: Why does it take a while for a real lava lamp to start bubbling after it is switched on?
a: The wax has to warm up first
The water has to freeze first
The lamp has to dry first
80484.e: At first the wax is solid and cold. Only when it is warm and soft do the blobs start to rise.
80484.m: A lava lamp needs time for the wax to warm up.

80485.q: Why should you not shake a warm lava lamp?
80485.e: When shaken, wax and liquid mix into tiny droplets. The lamp can then stay cloudy for a long time.
80485.m: Never shake a warm lava lamp.

80486.q: Where does the lava lamp get its name from?
a: It is filled with real lava
It was invented on a volcano
It gets as hot as lava
80486.e: The slowly flowing blobs of wax look like glowing lava from a volcano. That is why it is called a lava lamp.
80486.m: The wax blobs in a lava lamp look like lava.

80487.q: What can you easily use to grow crystals at home?
80487.e: You dissolve a lot of salt or sugar in water. As the water slowly evaporates, crystals grow from it.
80487.m: You can grow crystals from salt water or sugar water.

80488.q: Why do you dissolve the salt in warm water to grow crystals?
a: The salt turns colourful in it
The salt turns sweet in it
The salt goes hard in it
80488.e: Warm water can take up more salt than cold. The more salt is dissolved, the better the crystals grow.
80488.m: More salt dissolves in warm water.

80489.q: What do you hang in the salt solution so that crystals grow on it?
80489.e: You tie a piece of string to a pencil and lay the pencil across the glass. The crystals form on the string.
80489.m: Crystals grow on a string in the salt solution.

80490.q: How long does it take for nice crystals to grow?
80490.e: Crystals grow slowly while the water evaporates. So you need patience and should check every day.
80490.m: Growing crystals takes several days of patience.

80491.q: Where is the best place to put the glass with the crystal solution?
80491.e: Crystals grow best when the glass is not moved. Shaking disturbs their growth.
80491.m: Crystals grow best in a quiet place.

80492.q: What are the large sugar crystals you can put in tea called?
80492.e: Rock sugar forms when sugar slowly crystallises out of a solution. This produces large, clear crystals.
80492.m: Rock sugar is made of large sugar crystals.

80493.q: How many arms does a snow crystal have?
80493.e: Snow crystals are ice crystals. Because of the way ice is built, snowflakes have six arms or six points.
80493.m: A snow crystal has six arms.

80495.q: What is rock crystal made of?
80495.e: Rock crystal is clear, transparent quartz. Especially beautiful pieces are found in the Swiss Alps.
80495.m: Rock crystal is made of quartz.

80496.q: What colour is table salt in the tub?
80496.e: A single pure salt crystal is actually transparent. Lots of small grains together look white.

80497.q: Why did people in the past put meat and fish in salt?
80497.e: Salt draws water out of food. Without water, bacteria can hardly multiply, so salted food goes off less quickly.
80497.m: Salt makes meat and fish keep longer.

80498.q: Which animals like to lick a salt lick in the barn?
80498.e: Cows need salt, but they find too little of it in grass. That is why they get a salt lick in the barn or in the field.
80498.m: Cows like to lick a salt lick.

80499.q: Which bake is often sprinkled with coarse grains of salt?
80499.e: Pretzels are sprinkled with coarse salt before baking. The other bakes are usually sweet or have no salt crust.
80499.m: Pretzels are sprinkled with coarse salt.

80500.q: What is salt that is mined deep in the earth called?
80500.e: A very long time ago, seas dried up and left layers of salt behind. This salt in the ground is called rock salt.
80500.m: Salt from the earth is called rock salt.

80501.q: What do you use to sprinkle salt on your food at the table?
80501.e: A salt cellar has little holes at the top. That way only a little salt lands on the food.
80501.m: You season food at the table with a salt cellar.

80502.q: How much salt should you use with your food?
80502.e: The body needs some salt. But too much salt is unhealthy, so use it sparingly.

a: Flashes from a thunderstorm far away
81286.e: With heat lightning, you see the light of flashes that are very far away. They are completely normal thunderstorm flashes.
81286.m: Heat lightning comes from a distant thunderstorm.

81287.q: Why do you hear no thunder with heat lightning?
a: The storm is too far away
The wind blows the thunder away
81287.e: The sound of thunder does not travel as far as the light of the lightning. That is why you only see the flashes.
81287.m: You see distant light, but you do not hear distant thunder.

81288.q: When do we often see heat lightning in Switzerland?
81288.e: In Switzerland, thunderstorms happen mainly in summer. In the evening you can see their distant flashes well in the dark sky.
81288.m: You often see heat lightning on summer evenings.

81289.q: From what distance can you usually no longer hear a storm's thunder?
81289.e: You can usually only hear thunder up to about 15 to 20 kilometres away. You can see the light of lightning much further.

81290.q: With heat lightning, what do you often see instead of the flash itself?
a: The glow reflected in the clouds
81290.e: The flash itself is often hidden behind clouds or the horizon. You then only see the clouds light up briefly.
81290.m: With heat lightning, often only the clouds light up.

81291.q: Why do you mainly see heat lightning at night?
a: The faint glow stands out in the dark
The moon makes the clouds glow
81291.e: The distant glow is faint. In bright daylight you hardly see it, but in the dark night sky you see it well.
81291.m: You see heat lightning best in the dark.

81292.q: Where in the sky do you usually see heat lightning?
81292.e: The thunderstorm is far away. That is why it lights up low on the horizon.
81292.m: Heat lightning usually flickers on the horizon.

81293.q: What should you do if you suddenly hear thunder after seeing heat lightning?
a: Find shelter in a house or car
81293.e: If you can hear thunder, the storm is already close enough for lightning to strike. Then you find shelter at once.
81293.m: If you hear thunder, find shelter.

a: Rain with small grains of ice
81294.e: In drizzle, lots of tiny droplets fall. You hardly feel them one by one.
81294.m: Drizzle is made of very fine drops.

81295.q: How big are the droplets in drizzle?
81295.e: Drizzle droplets are tiny. Normal raindrops are usually much bigger.

81296.q: What does the sky usually look like when it is drizzling?
81296.e: Drizzle usually falls from a flat, grey layer of cloud that hangs low over the land.
81296.m: When it drizzles, the sky is grey.

81297.q: How do drizzle droplets fall compared with big raindrops?
81297.e: Small droplets are light and are strongly slowed down by the air. They almost float down.
81297.m: The smaller a drop is, the more slowly it falls.

81298.q: How long can it drizzle in Switzerland?
a: Only during a flash of lightning
81298.e: It can drizzle for a long time from a thick, low layer of cloud. Sometimes it does not stop for hours.
81298.m: Drizzle can last a very long time.

81300.q: How much water does drizzle usually bring?
81300.e: Because the droplets are so small, drizzle usually only adds up to a little water.
81300.m: Drizzle usually brings only a little water.

81301.q: How does drizzle feel on your skin?
81301.e: The droplets are so fine that you can hardly feel more than a damp breath of air.

81302.q: How hot does a flash of lightning get?
81302.e: A flash of lightning heats the air to about 30,000 degrees. That is much hotter than the surface of the sun.
81302.m: Lightning is hotter than the surface of the sun.

81303.q: How long does a flash of lightning last?
81303.e: A flash of lightning only lasts a fraction of a second. Sometimes it flickers several times in quick succession.
81303.m: Lightning is over in a flash.

81304.q: What should you do if a thunderstorm comes while you are swimming?
a: Get out of the water at once
81304.e: In the water you are the highest point, and water conducts electricity. That is why you must get out at once in a thunderstorm.
81304.m: In a thunderstorm, get out of the water at once.

81305.q: Roughly how often a year does lightning strike the transmitter tower on the Säntis?
81305.e: The tall tower on the Säntis strongly attracts lightning. Scientists measure the strikes there.
81305.m: Lightning can strike the same place very often.

81306.q: Why are you fairly safe in a car during a thunderstorm?
a: The metal body carries the current round the outside
The rubber tyres protect you from the current
81306.e: The current flows over the car's metal body into the ground. Inside you are protected as long as you do not touch anything metal.
81306.m: In a closed car you are protected from lightning.

81307.q: Why should you not stand under a lone tree in a thunderstorm?
81307.e: A lone tall tree is often the highest point for miles around. Lightning likes to strike there.
81307.m: Never stand under a lone tree in a thunderstorm.

a: Lightning heats the air in an instant
Two clouds bump into each other
81308.e: Lightning makes the air very hot in an instant. The air expands with a bang, and we hear that as thunder.
81308.m: Thunder is caused by the hot air of the lightning.

81309.q: You count 9 seconds between the lightning and the thunder. Roughly how far away is the storm?
81309.e: Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre. 9 seconds divided by 3 gives 3 kilometres.
81309.m: Count the seconds and divide by three to get the distance in kilometres.

81310.q: Why does thunder often rumble for a long time instead of just banging once?
a: The sound comes from many points along the long flash
Several clouds thunder one after another
The rain makes the bang louder
The wind carries the bang round in a circle
81310.e: A flash of lightning is often several kilometres long. The sound from the parts further away arrives later, so it rumbles for a long time.
81310.m: Long rumbling comes from the long path of the lightning.

81311.q: Which Germanic god of thunder is Thursday named after?
81311.e: Donar was the god of thunder for the Germanic peoples; in the north he was called Thor. Thursday is named after him.
81311.m: Thursday is named after the thunder god Thor.

81312.q: What is the name of the Norse god who makes thunder with his hammer?
81312.e: In the old legends from Scandinavia, Thor hurls his hammer. Then there is thunder in the sky.
81312.m: Thor is the thunder god of the Norse legends.

81313.q: What does it mean if the lightning and the crash of thunder come at the same time?
81313.e: If lightning and thunder come almost at the same time, the lightning is only a few hundred metres away.
81313.m: If it crashes straight after the lightning, the storm is very close.

81314.q: How long should you stay under shelter after the last thunder?
81314.e: Lightning can still strike even at the end of a thunderstorm. That is why you wait about half an hour after the last thunder.
81314.m: After the last thunder, wait another half hour.

81315.q: Can you hear thunder in Switzerland in winter too?
81315.e: Thunderstorms happen mainly in summer. But occasionally there is a thunderstorm in winter too, sometimes even while it is snowing.
81315.m: It can sometimes thunder in winter too.

81316.q: What is the scale called that divides wind into forces from 0 to 12?
81316.e: The Englishman Francis Beaufort invented this scale for sailors about 200 years ago.
81316.m: Wind strength is measured on the Beaufort scale.

81317.q: What is the very strongest wind, force 12, called?
81317.e: Force 12 is the highest level. A wind like this is called a hurricane and causes great damage.
81317.m: The strongest storm is called a hurricane.

81318.q: What was the storm called that caused huge damage to forests in Switzerland on 26 December 1999?
81318.e: Lothar swept across Switzerland on St Stephen's Day 1999. It blew down millions of trees.
81318.m: Storm Lothar devastated many Swiss forests in 1999.

81319.q: What does a fast-flashing orange light on the shore of a Swiss lake mean?
81319.e: On many Swiss lakes, orange flashing lights warn of strong wind. The faster they flash, the more dangerous it is.
81319.m: Orange flashing at the lake warns of a storm.

81320.q: How does the orange light at the lake flash when a storm is coming?
81320.e: For a storm warning, the light flashes very fast, about 90 times a minute. For a strong wind warning it flashes more slowly.
81320.m: For a storm warning, the light flashes very fast.

a: A short, strong blast of wind
81321.e: In a gust, the wind suddenly becomes much stronger for a few seconds. Then it dies down again.
81321.m: A gust is a sudden blast of wind.

81322.q: How fast does the wind blow in a hurricane-force wind at least?
81322.e: From about 118 kilometres per hour, it is called force 12. That is as fast as a car on the motorway.
81322.m: A hurricane-force wind is as fast as a car on the motorway.

81323.q: Why should you not go into the forest during a storm?
a: Branches and trees can fall down
81323.e: Strong wind can tear off branches and blow down whole trees. That is why the forest is dangerous in a storm.
81323.m: Stay out of the forest in a storm.

81324.q: What should you do on a lake when there is a storm warning?
a: Go back to the shore at once
Go far out onto the lake
81324.e: A storm makes high waves and can tip boats over. That is why you head back to the shore at once when there is a warning.
81324.m: When there is a storm warning, go back to the shore at once.

81325.q: Are there two snowflakes that look exactly the same?
a: Yes, they all look the same
81325.e: Every snowflake grows a little differently on its way through the cloud. That is why none is exactly like another.

a: The many ice crystals reflect the light
81326.e: The many tiny crystal faces reflect all the colours of light. Together, that looks white to us.
81326.m: Snow is white because it reflects all the light.

81327.q: Why is it so quiet outside after fresh snow has fallen?
81327.e: There is a lot of air between the snowflakes. That is why fresh snow soaks up sounds like a sponge.
81327.m: Fresh snow makes the world quiet.

81328.e: Snowflakes grow high up in cold clouds. When they are heavy enough, they fall down.

81329.q: What does an ice crystal start to grow around in a cloud?
a: A grain of sand from the beach
81329.e: Tiny specks of dust float in the air. Water vapour freezes onto them and a crystal starts to grow.
81329.m: A snow crystal grows around a speck of dust.

81330.q: In what weather do especially big snowflakes fall?
a: When it is just around zero degrees
81330.e: At just around zero degrees, the crystals are a little wet. They stick together into big flakes.
81330.m: Big flakes fall when it is just around zero degrees.

a: Little pellets of snow and ice
81331.e: Graupel is small, round grains. They fall from shower clouds, usually when it is cool.
81331.m: Graupel is little grains of snow and ice.

81332.e: Graupel pellets are as small as pinheads or small peas.
81332.m: Graupel pellets are only a few millimetres big.

81333.q: How is graupel different from hail?
81333.e: Hailstones are hard and can get big. Graupel is small and soft and can easily be squashed.
81333.m: Graupel is smaller and softer than hail.

81334.q: What do graupel pellets do when they land on a hard road?
81334.e: Graupel pellets are round and light. On hard ground they bounce like little balls.

81335.q: What kind of weather do graupel showers often belong to in Switzerland?
81335.e: In April, sun, rain and cold change quickly. Then there are often short showers with graupel.
81335.m: Graupel often comes with changeable April weather.

81336.e: Graupel is white and not see-through because there is a lot of air in the pellets.

81337.q: What does graupel form from in the cloud?
81337.e: In the cold cloud, tiny water droplets freeze onto snowflakes. This is how the white pellets form.
81337.m: Graupel forms from snow and frozen droplets.

81338.q: Does graupel usually damage cars and roofs?
a: Yes, it makes everything wet and rusty
81338.e: Graupel is light and soft. It falls more slowly than hail and so rarely causes damage.

a: A smooth layer of ice on roads and paths
81339.e: With black ice, a thin, smooth layer of ice covers the ground. It is very easy to slip on it.
81339.m: Black ice is a smooth layer of ice on the ground.

81340.q: When does black ice often form?
a: When rain falls on frozen ground
81340.e: If rain falls on ground that is colder than zero degrees, it freezes into ice at once.
81340.m: Rain on frozen ground turns into black ice.

81341.q: Why can you often hardly see black ice?
a: It is as clear as glass
It is only there at night
81341.e: Black ice is completely clear and thin. You see the dark ground underneath and hardly notice the ice.
81341.m: Black ice is so clear that you can hardly see it.

81342.q: What does the winter road service spread on the roads against black ice?
81342.e: Salt makes the ice melt, even when it is a little below zero degrees.
81342.m: Road salt helps against black ice.

81343.q: What is spread on pavements so that people do not slip?
81343.e: Grit does not melt the ice. But the small stones make the ground rough so that shoes can grip.
81343.m: Grit makes slippery paths less slippery.

81344.q: Where does the road often freeze first in winter?
81344.e: Bridges are cooled by cold air from above and below. That is why they are often slippery sooner than the rest of the road.
81344.m: Bridges are often the first to be slippery.

81345.q: What helps on your shoes when it is slippery?
81345.e: Spikes and shoe chains have small metal points. They dig into the ice.

81346.q: What is the best way to walk on black ice?
a: With small steps like a penguin
81346.e: With small, flat steps your weight stays over your feet. That way you slip less.
81346.m: On black ice, walk like a penguin.

81347.q: At what temperature should you expect black ice?
81347.e: Water freezes at zero degrees. If the ground is that cold or colder, black ice can form.
81347.m: Around zero degrees, the roads get dangerous.

81348.q: What shape is a big falling raindrop?
a: Like a bread roll, flat underneath
Like a teardrop with a point
81348.e: As it falls, the air pushes against the drop from below. That is why it becomes flat underneath and looks like a bread roll.
81348.m: Raindrops are not shaped like teardrops.

81349.q: What happens to raindrops that get too big?
81349.e: From about 6 millimetres, a drop can no longer hold together. It then bursts into several smaller drops.
81349.m: Raindrops that are too big burst.

81350.q: Roughly how fast does a normal raindrop fall?
a: As fast as a racing car
81350.e: A normal raindrop falls at about 20 kilometres per hour. That is about as fast as a bike.
81350.m: A raindrop falls about as fast as a bike goes.

81351.q: What do you use to measure how much it has rained?
81351.e: A rain gauge is a container that catches the rainwater. It shows how much rain has fallen.
81351.m: A rain gauge catches the rain.

81352.q: What shape are very small raindrops?
81352.e: Small drops up to about one millimetre are held together into balls by their surface.

81353.q: What happens when lots of tiny droplets in a cloud run together?
81353.e: Cloud droplets are tiny. Only when very many run together is a raindrop heavy enough to fall.
81353.m: A raindrop is made from very many cloud droplets.

81354.q: Where does most of the water evaporate that later becomes rain?
81354.e: The oceans cover most of the Earth. That is where the sun makes the most water evaporate.
81354.m: Most rainwater comes from the oceans.

81355.q: Where does a weathercock usually sit?
a: On top of a church spire
81355.e: The weathercock sits high up so that the wind can reach it easily and everyone can see it.
81355.m: The weathercock often sits on the church tower.

a: Where the wind is blowing from
81356.e: The weathercock turns with the wind. That way you can see the wind direction.
81356.m: The weathercock shows the wind direction.

81357.q: Which way does a weathercock's beak point?
a: Towards where the wind is coming from
Towards where the wind is blowing to
81357.e: The wide tail is pushed away by the wind. That is why the head turns right into the wind.
81357.m: The weathercock faces into the wind.

81358.q: What is a weathercock usually made of?
81358.e: Weathercocks are usually made of sheet metal or copper. That way they can stand up to wind, rain and snow for many years.
81358.m: A weathercock is usually made of metal.

81359.q: Which story from the Bible does the cockerel on the church tower remind us of?
a: Peter, who denied Jesus before the cock crowed
81359.e: Jesus said Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed. According to the story, that is what happened.
81359.m: The cockerel on the church tower reminds us of Peter.

81360.q: Roughly how long have there been weathercocks on church towers?
81360.e: As early as around the year 820, a bishop in Brescia in Italy had a copper cockerel put on a church tower.
81360.m: Weathercocks have existed for over a thousand years.

81361.q: What is often fixed underneath a weathercock?
a: The letters of the compass points
81361.e: Under the cockerel there are often the letters N, E, S and W. That way you can read the wind direction exactly.
81361.m: The compass points help you read the weathercock.

81362.q: What is the general name for a turning figure on a roof that shows the wind?
81362.e: A weather vane turns with the wind. The weathercock is a particularly well-known weather vane.
81362.m: The weathercock is a weather vane.

81363.q: Where do you often see a windsock?
81363.e: Airfields are required to have a windsock. It shows the wind for take-offs and landings.

81364.q: What colours is a windsock usually?
81364.e: Windsocks usually have red and white or orange and white stripes.
81364.m: A windsock usually has red and white stripes.

81365.q: What does it mean if a windsock is stretched out completely straight?
a: There is no wind at all
81365.e: The stronger the wind blows, the more it fills the windsock. Fully stretched out means strong wind.
81365.m: A stretched-out windsock shows strong wind.

81366.q: Why is there sometimes a windsock on a motorway bridge?
a: It shows the way to the exit
81366.e: On high bridges, strong wind from the side can put cars and lorries in danger. The windsock warns drivers.
81366.m: On bridges, the windsock warns of crosswinds.

81367.q: Which way does the tip of a windsock point?
a: The way the wind is blowing to
The way the wind is coming from
81367.e: The wind blows into the big opening. So the tip points in the direction the wind is blowing.
81367.m: The tip of the windsock points with the wind.

81369.q: Why does a windsock have such eye-catching colours?
a: So pilots can see it from high up
So birds do not sit on it
81369.e: Pilots need to spot the windsock from the air. The stripes stand out well against grass and sky.
81369.m: A windsock must be visible from high up.

81370.q: What is a windsock made of?
81370.e: A windsock is a tube made of cloth. That is the only way the wind can fill it and turn it.
81370.m: A windsock is a cloth tube.

81371.q: Why do pilots need to know the wind direction?
a: Aeroplanes take off and land into the wind
Aeroplanes only fly with a tailwind
The wind shows the way to the destination
The wind forecasts the weather at the destination
81371.e: A headwind gives the aeroplane more lift on take-off and slows it down on landing. That is why the runway is used facing into the wind.
81371.m: Aeroplanes take off and land into the wind.

81372.q: Which frog used to be kept as a “weather frog”?
81372.e: In the past, people put tree frogs in jars and hoped they would give away the weather.
81372.m: The weather frog was a tree frog.

81373.q: What did people put in the weather frog's jar?
81373.e: There was a little ladder in the jar. People looked to see whether the frog was sitting at the top or the bottom.
81373.m: The weather frog had a little ladder in its jar.

81374.q: What did people think when the weather frog climbed up the ladder?
81374.e: If the frog sat at the top, people expected dry, fine weather. If it sat at the bottom, they expected rain.
81374.m: A frog at the top of the ladder was supposed to mean fine weather.

81375.q: Why does a tree frog climb upwards in fine weather?
a: Because the insects fly higher then
Because it can forecast the weather
Because it is too warm at the bottom
Because it wants to catch the sun
81375.e: In sunshine, insects fly higher, and the frog climbs after them. So it shows the weather right now, but does not forecast it.
81375.m: The tree frog climbs after its food.

81376.q: In German, who is jokingly called a “Wetterfrosch” (weather frog) today?
a: Children who play in the rain
81376.e: People who explain the weather on TV or radio are sometimes jokingly called weather frogs.
81376.m: Weather experts are jokingly called weather frogs.

81377.q: What is the federal office called that forecasts the weather in Switzerland?
81377.e: MeteoSwiss is the federal weather service. It measures the weather in many places and warns of severe weather.

81378.q: What are the well-known weather prophets from the Muota valley called?
81378.e: The Wetterschmöcker of the Muota valley forecast the weather using old signs from nature. They make their forecasts twice a year.
81378.m: The Wetterschmöcker of the Muota valley forecast the weather using signs from nature.

81379.q: Are you allowed to simply catch a tree frog in Switzerland and put it in a jar?
81379.e: In Switzerland all frogs are protected. The tree frog has also become rare.
81379.m: Tree frogs are protected and stay in the wild.

81380.q: What colour is a tree frog usually?
81380.e: The tree frog is usually light green. With the sticky pads on its toes it climbs well on leaves.
81380.m: The tree frog is bright green.

81381.e: Wood is the hard material in the trunk and branches of trees. Trees are felled and sawn into planks.
81381.m: Wood grows in the trees of the forest.

81382.q: What can you tell from the rings in a tree trunk?
81382.e: A tree forms a new annual ring every year. If you count the rings, you know how old the tree is.
81382.m: Each annual ring stands for one year of the tree's life.

81383.q: What does a dry piece of wood do in water?
81383.e: Dry wood is lighter than the same amount of water. That is why it floats on top.

81384.q: What is the craftsperson who makes furniture from wood called?
81384.e: The joiner saws, planes and glues wood into tables, cupboards and doors.
81384.m: A joiner makes furniture from wood.

81385.q: Which conifer in Switzerland loses its needles in autumn?
81385.e: In autumn the larch turns its needles golden yellow and drops them. Larch wood is very hard and lasts a long time outdoors.
81385.m: The larch has no needles in winter.

81386.q: What do Swiss wrestlers (Schwinger) fight on?
81386.e: Sawdust is produced when wood is sawn. It is soft and protects the wrestlers when they fall.
81386.m: In Swiss wrestling, soft sawdust covers the ring.

81387.q: Which tree grows most often in Swiss forests?
81387.e: The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests. Its wood is often used for building.
81387.m: The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests.

81388.q: Why doesn't a wooden spoon in a hot pan get as hot as a metal spoon?
81388.e: Wood passes on heat only very slowly. That is why you can easily hold a wooden spoon.

81389.q: What happens to wood that stays wet for a long time?
81389.e: Fungi and tiny living things break down wet wood. It becomes soft and crumbly.

81390.q: What is glass mainly made from?
81390.e: Glass is made mainly from quartz sand. It is heated very strongly with other substances and melted.
81390.m: Glass is made from melted sand.

81391.q: About how hot does it have to be to melt glass?
81391.e: To melt sand into glass, you need a furnace at well over 1000 degrees. That is much hotter than an oven.
81391.m: Glass is only made in very great heat.

81392.q: What often happens when a drinking glass falls on a hard floor?
81392.e: Glass is hard but brittle. A hard knock breaks it into pieces.
81392.m: Glass is hard, but it breaks easily.

81393.q: What is a craftsperson called who shapes hot glass into vases using a pipe?
81393.e: The glassblower picks up liquid glass on a long pipe. Then they blow into it, and the glass becomes a ball or a vase.
81393.m: A glassblower shapes vases with their breath.

81394.q: Which part of a house is usually made of glass?
81394.e: Window panes are made of glass so that light comes into the house. Wind and rain stay outside.
81394.m: Light comes into the house through glass window panes.

81395.q: Why should you not pick up broken glass with your bare hands?
81395.e: The edges of broken glass are as sharp as a knife. It is better to sweep it up with a dustpan and brush.

81396.q: What happens to glass when it is heated very strongly?
81396.e: In great heat, glass becomes soft and thick like honey. Then it can be shaped.
81396.m: Hot glass becomes soft and can be shaped.

81397.q: What is behind the glass of a mirror?
81397.e: On the back of the mirror glass is a very thin layer of silver or aluminium. It reflects the light.
81397.m: A mirror has a shiny layer of metal at the back.

81398.q: What are colourful marbles for playing often made of?
81398.e: Many marbles are little balls of coloured glass.
81398.m: Many marbles are made of coloured glass.

81399.q: Why are railway tracks made of steel?
a: Steel is very strong and hard
81399.e: Steel is a very strong metal. The rails have to carry heavy trains without breaking.

81400.q: What does a piece of metal usually feel like when you touch it?
81400.e: Metal quickly carries the warmth of your hand away. That is why it feels cool.
81400.m: Metal feels cool because it carries heat away quickly.

81401.q: Why is there a metal wire inside an electric cable?
81401.e: Electricity flows well through metals such as copper. That is why the wires in cables are made of metal.

81402.q: What happens to metal in very great heat?
81402.e: If metal is heated strongly enough, it becomes liquid. Then it can be poured into moulds.
81402.m: In great heat, metal becomes liquid.

81403.q: What does freshly polished metal look like?
81403.e: Metals reflect a lot of light. That is why they shine when they are clean and polished.
81403.m: Polished metal shines in the light.

81404.q: Which device can you use to find metal hidden in the ground?
81404.e: A metal detector beeps when there is metal underneath it. This is how you find coins or nails in the ground.
81404.m: A metal detector beeps at metal in the ground.

a: A long thin thread of metal
81405.e: A wire is metal that has been drawn out long and thin. You can bend it.
81405.m: A wire is a thin thread of metal.

81406.q: What are most metals obtained from?
81406.e: Ore is a rock that contains metal. It is melted in a furnace to get the metal out.
81406.m: Metals are obtained from ore in rock.

81407.q: What are forks and knives usually made of?
81407.e: Cutlery is usually made of stainless steel. This is a metal that is strong and does not rust.
81407.m: Cutlery is usually made of stainless steel.

81409.q: What is plastic usually made from?
81409.e: Most plastics are made in factories from crude oil.
81409.m: Most plastics are made from crude oil.

81410.q: What is a good property of plastic?
a: It is light and easy to shape
It is as heavy as iron
81410.e: Plastic is light and can be shaped into almost any form. That is why boxes, toys and much more are made from it.
81410.m: Plastic is light and easy to shape.

81411.q: Why is plastic a problem in nature?
81411.e: Plastic does not rot like leaves. It stays in nature for many hundreds of years.
81411.m: Plastic stays in nature for a very long time.

81412.q: Does plastic grow in nature or is it made by people?
81412.e: Plastic is a synthetic, man-made material. People make it in factories.
81412.m: Plastic is a man-made material from the factory.

81413.q: Which object is usually made of plastic?
81413.e: The handle and bristles of a toothbrush are usually made of plastic. It is light and does not get soggy.
81413.m: Most toothbrushes are made of plastic.

81414.q: What happens to many plastics when they get very hot?
81414.e: Many plastics go soft in the heat and melt. That is why you don't put plastic on a hot hob.
81414.m: Many plastics go soft in the heat.

81415.q: What are fleece jumpers usually made of?
81415.e: Fleece is made of fine plastic fibres. The fabric is light, soft and warm.
81415.m: Fleece is a warm fabric made of plastic fibres.

81416.q: Why is there a plastic coating around an electric cable?
81416.e: Plastic does not let electricity through. The coating protects us when we touch the cable.
81416.m: A plastic coating protects us from electricity.

81417.q: What is paper usually made from?
81417.e: To make paper, wood is broken down into fine fibres. These are mixed with water and pressed into thin sheets.
81417.m: Paper is usually made from wood fibres.

81418.q: What did the ancient Egyptians write on before there was paper?
81418.e: Papyrus was made from the stems of a plant by the Nile. Our word paper comes from it.
81418.m: The ancient Egyptians wrote on papyrus.

81419.q: What do you call thick, stiff paper for boxes?
81419.e: Cardboard is much thicker and stiffer than writing paper. Boxes and packaging are made from it.
81419.m: Boxes are often made of stiff cardboard.

81420.q: What can be made again from waste paper?
81420.e: The fibres in waste paper can be used again. That way less wood is needed for new paper.
81420.m: New paper is made from waste paper.

81421.q: Why must paper not be near a burning candle?
81421.e: Paper is thin and dry. It burns very quickly even from a small flame.

81422.q: Where does natural rubber come from?
a: From the sap of a tree
81422.e: Natural rubber is made from the milky sap of the rubber tree. The bark is cut and the sap is collected.
81422.m: Natural rubber comes from the sap of the rubber tree.

a: It is as hard as stone
81423.e: You can pull and squeeze rubber. Afterwards it goes back to its old shape.

81424.q: What do you use a rubber for?
81424.e: A rubber rubs pencil marks off the paper. That is where its name comes from.
81424.m: You remove pencil marks with a rubber.

81425.q: Why do people like wearing wellies in the rain?
a: Rubber does not let water through
81425.e: Rubber is waterproof. In wellies your feet stay dry even in puddles.

81426.q: What is the milky sap of the rubber tree called?
81426.e: The white sap of the rubber tree is called latex. Natural rubber is made from it.
81426.m: The sap of the rubber tree is called latex.

81427.q: Where does the rubber tree originally grow?
81427.e: The rubber tree comes from the rainforest by the Amazon. Today it is grown mainly in Asia.
81427.m: The rubber tree comes from the Amazon rainforest.

81428.q: What is a balloon usually made of?
81428.e: Balloons are usually made of thin rubber. That is why you can blow them up big.
81428.m: A balloon is made of thin rubber.

81429.q: Which part of a trainer is usually made of rubber?
81429.e: A rubber sole does not slip easily. It is springy and lasts a long time.
81429.m: Rubber soles don't slip so easily.

81430.q: Which animal does most wool come from?
81430.e: Sheep have a thick, curly coat. Wool is made from it.

81431.q: What do you do with wool to turn it into a thread?
81431.e: When spinning, the wool fibres are twisted into a long thread. In the past this was done with a spinning wheel.
81431.m: Wool is spun into a thread.

81432.q: What do you use to knit a woolly jumper?
81432.e: With two knitting needles, the wool is looped into stitches. Row by row, a piece of fabric grows.
81432.m: Knitting needles turn wool into stitches.

81433.q: Why does a woolly jumper keep you so nice and warm?
a: It traps a lot of air
81433.e: A lot of air gets caught between the curly wool fibres. This air holds in the body's warmth.
81433.m: The air in wool keeps us warm.

81434.q: Which animal from South America also gives very fine wool?
81434.e: Alpacas come from the Andes. Their wool is soft and warm, and there are alpacas on Swiss farms too.
81434.m: The alpaca gives soft, fine wool.

81435.q: What can happen to a woolly jumper if you wash it too hot?
81435.e: In hot water with lots of rubbing, the wool fibres mat together. The jumper shrinks and gets smaller.
81435.m: Wash wool cool, otherwise it shrinks.

81436.q: What is a thick fabric made of tightly pressed wool called?
81436.e: To make felt, wet wool is pressed and rubbed until the fibres hold firmly together. Slippers, for example, are made from it.
81436.m: Felt is made from pressed wool.

81437.q: Which part of the cotton plant provides the fibres?
81437.e: The seeds of the plant are surrounded by white, fluffy hairs. These hairs are picked and spun into yarn.
81437.m: Cotton fibres grow on the seeds of the plant.

81438.q: Why is cotton not grown in fields in Switzerland?
a: It is too cold for it
81438.e: Cotton needs a lot of warmth and a long warm season each year. Switzerland is too cool for it.
81438.m: Cotton only grows in warm countries.

81439.q: Which trousers are usually made of cotton?
81439.e: Jeans are made of a strong cotton fabric. It is usually dyed blue.
81439.m: Jeans are made of strong cotton fabric.

81440.q: Why do people like wearing cotton T-shirts in summer?
81440.e: Cotton is soft and soaks up moisture well. That is why it feels pleasant on the skin.

81441.q: What are the little sticks with soft cotton tips at both ends called?
81441.e: Cotton wool is made from cotton. Cotton buds are used, for example, for crafts or personal care.
81441.m: Cotton buds have tips of soft cotton wool.

81442.q: Which city in eastern Switzerland became world-famous for embroidery on cotton fabric?
81442.e: Over 100 years ago, much of the world's embroidery came from the St Gallen area. It was often stitched onto fine cotton fabrics.
81442.m: St Gallen is famous for its embroidery.

81443.q: What colour are cotton fibres usually?
81443.e: Cotton on the plant looks like white cotton wool balls. Coloured fabrics are only dyed later.

81444.e: Clay is a fine, damp earth. It is easy to knead and shape.

81445.q: What do you do with shaped clay to make it really hard?
a: You fire it in a kiln
81445.e: In a very hot kiln, the clay becomes as hard as stone. Only then is it ceramics.
81445.m: Clay is fired hard in a kiln.

81446.q: What is the craftsperson who makes crockery from clay called?
81446.e: The potter shapes cups, plates and jugs from clay and then fires them.
81446.m: The potter makes crockery from clay.

81447.q: On which spinning disc are round pots shaped?
81447.e: The potter's wheel spins fast. With their hands, the potter pulls the clay up into a round pot.
81447.m: Round pots are shaped on the potter's wheel.

81448.q: What is the fine white ceramic for beautiful cups called?
81448.e: Porcelain is an especially fine and hard ceramic. It is white and sometimes almost translucent.

81449.q: What are bathroom tiles usually made of?
81449.e: Tiles are fired ceramic slabs. They are hard and easy to clean with water.
81449.m: Bathroom tiles are usually made of ceramic.

81450.q: What is the shiny layer on ceramic crockery called?
81450.e: The glaze is a thin, glass-like layer. It makes the crockery smooth, shiny and watertight.
81450.m: A glaze makes ceramics smooth and shiny.

81451.q: What are red roof tiles usually made of?
81451.e: Roof tiles are shaped from clay and fired in a kiln. They keep out rain and snow for many years.
81451.m: Red roof tiles are made of fired clay.

81452.e: Leather is animal skin that has been specially treated. This makes it last and stops it rotting.
81452.m: Leather is made from animal skin.

81453.q: What do you call turning animal skin into leather?
81453.e: In tanning, the skin is treated with special substances. Afterwards it is soft, strong and long-lasting.

81454.q: What is the craftsperson who makes and mends shoes called?
81454.e: The shoemaker, also called a cobbler, often works with leather. They sew shoes and replace old soles.

81455.q: Which object is often made of leather?
81455.e: Leather is strong and flexible at the same time. That is why belts, bags and shoes are often made from it.
81455.m: Many belts are made of leather.

81456.q: Which animal does most of the world's leather come from?
81456.e: Most leather is made from the skin of cattle. The skin is thick and large.

81457.q: What do you use to look after leather shoes so that they shine?
81457.e: Shoe polish makes the leather soft and protects it from wet. After polishing, the shoes shine.
81457.m: Shoe polish cares for leather and makes it shine.

81458.q: What was the outer cover of a football made of in the past?
81458.e: In the past, footballs were sewn from pieces of leather. Today they are mostly made of plastic.
81458.m: Old footballs were sewn from leather.

81459.q: What lies on a horse's back when riding and is often made of leather?
81459.e: The saddle is usually made of strong leather. The rider sits on it safely and comfortably.
81459.m: A saddle is usually made of leather.

81460.e: For concrete, cement, sand, gravel and water are mixed. After a while the mixture becomes rock hard.
81460.m: Concrete is made of cement, gravel and water.

81461.q: What happens to fresh concrete after a while?
81461.e: The cement combines with the water. This makes the concrete as hard as stone.
81461.m: Fresh concrete becomes rock hard over time.

81462.q: Which vehicle with a turning drum brings concrete to the building site?
81462.e: The drum of the cement mixer turns while it drives. This keeps the concrete liquid until it arrives.
81462.m: The cement mixer turns its drum while driving.

81463.q: What is put into concrete to make it even stronger?
81463.e: Steel bars in concrete make it very strong. This is called reinforced concrete.
81463.m: Steel bars make concrete even stronger.

81464.q: Which ancient people already knew a kind of concrete?
81464.e: The Romans built with a kind of concrete about 2000 years ago. One example is the huge dome of the Pantheon in Rome.
81464.m: Even the Romans built with a kind of concrete.

81465.e: Cement is a fine grey powder. Mixed with water it goes hard and holds sand and gravel together.
81465.m: Cement is a grey powder that goes hard with water.

81466.q: Which vehicle brings liquid concrete to the building site?
81466.e: The cement mixer has a big drum at the back. It turns so that the concrete doesn't go hard on the way.
81466.m: The cement mixer brings the concrete to the building site.

81467.e: Bees sweat out tiny flakes of wax from their bodies. They build their home from them.

81468.q: What do bees build from wax?
81468.e: Honeycombs are made of many six-sided cells of wax. Honey and pollen are stored in them.
81468.m: Bees build their honeycombs from wax.

81469.q: What is most candle wax made from today?
81469.e: Most candles are made of paraffin wax. This wax is made from crude oil.
81469.m: Most candles are made of paraffin wax.

81470.q: What happens to liquid wax when it cools down?
81470.e: Wax goes liquid in the warmth. When it cools down, it goes solid again.
81470.m: Liquid wax goes solid as it cools.

81471.q: What are some wheels of cheese coated with on the outside?
81471.e: A layer of wax protects the cheese from drying out and from mould. You don't eat it.
81471.m: Wax protects some cheeses from drying out.

81472.q: What do you rub on the underside of skis so that they glide better?
81472.e: Ski wax makes the underside of the skis smooth. Then they glide better over the snow.
81472.m: With ski wax, skis glide better.

81473.q: What is the thread in the middle of a candle called?
81473.e: The wick draws liquid wax upwards. There it burns with a flame.
81473.m: A candle's wick draws wax upwards.

81474.q: What do you call dipping a wick again and again into liquid wax?
81474.e: In candle dipping, the candle gets a little thicker with each dip. In Switzerland, people like to do this during Advent.
81474.m: In candle dipping, the candle gets thicker layer by layer.

81475.q: What does a layer of wax do to water on a surface?
a: It makes it run off in beads
81475.e: Wax does not like water. The drops run off in beads and don't soak in.
81475.m: Water drops run off wax in beads.

82262.e: When layers of rock are pushed together from the side, they bend. This makes a fold in the rock.
82262.m: A rock fold is made of bent layers of rock.

82263.q: What happens to layers of rock when they are pushed together from two sides?
82263.e: The layers cannot get out of the way and bend up and down. We say they are folded.
82263.m: Rock layers that are pushed together fold.

82265.q: Which Swiss mountain range in the north-west is made of many beautiful folds?
82265.e: The Jura is made of long, folded chains of limestone. That is why it is called the Folded Jura.
82265.m: The Jura is a fold mountain range.

82266.q: Which two big tectonic plates collided and folded up the Alps?
82266.e: The African Plate pushed against the European Plate. Layers of rock were folded and piled up into the Alps.
82266.m: Africa pushed against Europe, and that is how the Alps formed.

82267.q: Where in the mountains can you often see rock folds well?
82267.e: On steep rock faces the rock is exposed. You can see the bent layers well there.
82267.m: You can often see rock folds on rock faces.

82268.q: How long does it take for rock to bend into a big fold?
82268.e: Rock only moves very slowly. Big folds take millions of years to form.
82268.m: Rock folds form over millions of years.

82269.q: How do layers of rock lie at first, before they are folded?
a: Flat on top of each other
82269.e: Layers often form on the seabed and at first lie flat on top of each other. Only later can they be bent.
82269.m: Rock layers first lie flat on top of each other.

82270.q: Which is the highest mountain in Switzerland?
82270.e: No other summit in Switzerland is higher. It lies near the border with Italy.
82270.m: The Dufourspitze is the highest mountain in Switzerland.

82271.q: Roughly how high is the Dufourspitze?
82271.e: The Dufourspitze is 4634 metres high. That makes it the highest summit in Switzerland.
82271.m: The Dufourspitze is over 4000 metres high.

82272.q: Which big mountain massif does the Dufourspitze belong to?
82272.e: The Dufourspitze is the highest summit in the Monte Rosa massif. This massif has several summits over 4000 metres.
82272.m: The Dufourspitze belongs to Monte Rosa.

82273.q: Which summit is the highest point in Switzerland?
82273.e: The Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif is about 4634 metres high. It is named after General Henri Dufour.
82273.m: The Dufourspitze is the highest mountain in Switzerland.

82275.q: What covers the Dufourspitze all year round?
82275.e: At over 4600 metres it is always cold. That is why there is snow and ice there all year round.
82275.m: The Dufourspitze is covered in snow all year round.

82276.e: Lots of loose stones collect below rock faces. They form a steep slope, the scree slope.
82276.m: A scree slope is a slope of loose stones.

82277.q: Where do you usually find scree slopes?
82277.e: Stones break off the rock faces and fall down. They collect into a slope at the foot of the face.
82277.m: Scree slopes lie below rock faces.

82278.q: What breaks stones off the rocks, which then fall onto the scree slope?
82278.e: Water gets into cracks and freezes into ice. Ice needs more space and so breaks pieces off the rock, especially when it often freezes and thaws again.
82278.m: Freezing water breaks stones off the rock.

82279.q: Why is it dangerous to walk across a scree slope?
82279.e: The stones lie loosely on top of each other. If you step on them, they can slide away.
82279.m: On scree slopes, the stones slip easily.

82280.q: Which alpine animal likes living among the stones of scree slopes and whistles when there is danger?
82280.e: Marmots live in burrows among stones and meadows. When there is danger, they warn the others with a loud whistle.
82280.m: Marmots whistle when there is danger.

82281.q: What shape does a scree slope often have?
a: Like a cone or a fan
82281.e: The stones fall down at one spot and spread out downwards. This often makes a cone or a fan.
82281.m: A scree slope is often shaped like a cone.

82282.q: Where on a scree slope are the biggest stones usually found?
82282.e: Big, heavy stones roll further when they fall. That is why they usually lie at the foot of the slope.
82282.m: The biggest stones roll furthest down the slope.

82283.q: What is another word for a scree slope?
82283.e: A scree slope is also called a talus slope. Both mean a slope of loose rock debris.
82283.m: A scree slope is also called a talus slope.

a: An opening at the end of the glacier
A door to a ski hut
82284.e: At the lower end of a glacier there is often a big opening in the ice. Meltwater flows out there.
82284.m: A glacier portal is an opening at the end of the glacier.

82285.q: What comes out of a glacier portal?
82285.e: Meltwater collects under the glacier. It comes out at the glacier portal as a glacier stream.
82285.m: A glacier stream flows out of the glacier portal.

82286.q: What colour is the water from a glacier portal often?
82286.e: The water carries finely ground rock with it. That is why it looks cloudy and milky grey.

82287.q: What is the cloudy water called that flows out of the glacier portal?
82287.e: The water is full of the finest rock flour. Because it is so cloudy, it is called glacier milk.
82287.m: Cloudy glacier water is called glacier milk.

82288.q: Why should you not go into a glacier portal?
82288.e: The ice at the glacier portal is melting and is often brittle. Big pieces of ice can suddenly fall down.
82288.m: Ice can break off at the glacier portal.

82289.q: When does the most water flow out of a glacier portal?
82289.e: When it is warm, a lot of ice melts. That is why there is the most water in the glacier stream on summer afternoons.
82289.m: The most glacier water flows on summer afternoons.

82290.q: Which big river begins at a glacier in Valais?
82290.e: The Rhône rises at the Rhône Glacier in Valais. Its water comes from the glacier's meltwater.
82290.m: The Rhône begins at the Rhône Glacier.

82291.q: Why does a glacier portal change from year to year?
a: It is walled up with stones
82291.e: A glacier flows slowly and melts away at its end. That is why its portal keeps changing.

82292.e: A pass is a lower point between mountains. A path or road leads there from one valley to another.
82292.m: A mountain pass leads over the mountains.

82293.q: Which pass links the canton of Uri with Ticino?
82293.e: The Gotthard Pass leads from Andermatt in the canton of Uri to Airolo in Ticino. It is one of the best-known passes in the Alps.
82293.m: The Gotthard Pass links Uri with Ticino.

82294.q: Why are many passes closed in winter?
a: Because of floods in the sea
82294.e: In winter there is a lot of snow on the passes. Avalanches make the roads dangerous, so they are closed.
82294.m: Many passes are closed in winter because of snow.

82295.q: Which dogs is the Great St Bernard Pass famous for?
82295.e: The monks on the Great St Bernard bred St Bernard dogs. In the past the dogs helped to find travellers in the snow.
82295.m: St Bernard dogs come from the Great St Bernard.

82296.q: What is a house on a pass called where travellers used to find shelter?
82296.e: A hospice is a lodging on a pass. Travellers found food and a warm bed there.
82296.m: A hospice gave travellers shelter on the pass.

82297.q: What are the tight bends called that a road often uses to climb up to a pass?
82297.e: On steep slopes the road zigzags back and forth in many tight bends. These bends are called hairpin bends or switchbacks.
82297.m: Pass roads often have lots of hairpin bends.

82298.q: What was built so that people can cross the Gotthard safely in winter too?
82298.e: Today railway and road tunnels go through the Gotthard. That way you can get from north to south even when it snows.

82299.q: Which two things does a mountain pass connect?
82299.e: A pass leads up out of one valley and down into another valley on the other side. That is how it connects two valleys.

a: A very steep slope of rock
A flat stone by a stream
82300.e: A rock face is a steep, often almost vertical surface of rock. You find them on many mountains.
82300.m: A rock face is a steep slope of rock.

82301.q: Which famous rock face is in the Bernese Oberland?
82301.e: The Eiger North Face is about 1800 metres high. It is one of the best-known climbing walls in the Alps.
82301.m: The Eiger North Face is a famous rock face.

82302.q: Who climbs rock faces with a rope and a helmet?
82302.e: Climbers go up rock faces with a rope, harness and helmet. The rope protects them if they fall.
82302.m: Climbers secure themselves on the rock face with a rope.

82303.q: Which big bird of prey often builds its nest on rock faces?
82303.e: The golden eagle likes to build its eyrie on steep rock faces. There it is safe from enemies.
82303.m: The golden eagle likes to nest on rock faces.

82304.q: In which valley do the Staubbach Falls plunge over a high rock face?
82304.e: The Lauterbrunnen valley has very steep rock faces. Lots of waterfalls plunge down them, for example the Staubbach Falls.
82304.m: The Lauterbrunnen valley has high rock faces and waterfalls.

82305.q: Why do you need to be careful at the foot of a rock face?
a: The ground is made of glass
82305.e: Stones keep coming loose from a rock face. That is why it is dangerous at the foot of the face.
82305.m: Stones can fall down below rock faces.

82306.q: What is an easy climbing route with fixed steel cables and ladders called?
82306.e: On a via ferrata, steel cables, rungs and ladders are fixed to the rock. You clip yourself in with a special set and are protected that way.
82306.m: A via ferrata has fixed steel cables on the rock.

82307.q: Which animal with big curved horns climbs skilfully on rock faces?
82307.e: The ibex has hooves that grip well on rock. It climbs safely over steep rocks.
82307.m: The ibex climbs skilfully on rock.

82308.e: In a rockfall, stones come loose from a slope or a rock face. They fall or bounce down.

82309.q: What protects your head from falling stones when climbing?
82309.e: A hard helmet stops falling stones. That is why climbers and mountaineers wear a helmet.
82309.m: A helmet protects your head from falling stones.

82310.q: What is put up along mountain roads to protect cars from falling stones?
82310.e: Strong steel nets catch falling stones. That keeps roads and railway lines safer.

a: When ice in the rock thaws
When there is no wind in winter
When it has been dry for a long time
At night during a full moon
82311.e: Ice holds loose stones in place like glue. When it thaws, the stones come loose and fall down.
82311.m: There is often rockfall when things thaw.

82312.q: What should you shout if you kick a stone loose yourself?
82312.e: By shouting “Rock!” loudly, you warn people further down. Then they can protect themselves.
82312.m: If you kick a stone loose, shout “Rock!” loudly.

82313.q: What does a road sign with falling stones on it show?
82313.e: The sign warns of stones that can fall onto the road. You should not stop there.
82313.m: The sign with falling stones warns of rockfall.

82314.q: How should you behave on a path where there is a danger of falling rocks?
a: Stop for a long time and have a picnic
82314.e: Where stones can fall, you do not stand still. You keep walking briskly until you are out of the danger zone.
82314.m: Do not take a break in rockfall zones.

82315.q: What is a roof over a road called that protects it from stones and avalanches?
82315.e: A gallery is a strong concrete roof over the road, closed on the mountain side. Stones and avalanches slide over the top of it.
82315.m: A gallery protects roads from stones and avalanches.

a: A large area of lying snow
An ice rink in the village
82316.e: A snowfield is a large area of snow in the mountains. It often stays until well into the summer.
82316.m: A snowfield is a large area of snow in the mountains.

82317.q: Why is there still snow on high mountains even in summer?
a: Because it is colder up there
Because the sun does not shine there
Because the snow there is salty
82317.e: The higher you go, the colder it gets. That is why the snow melts more slowly up there and stays.
82317.m: It is colder high up, so the snow stays longer.

82318.q: Why is a steep snowfield dangerous when hiking?
82318.e: Snow can be hard and slippery. If you slip, you can slide down the slope.
82318.m: You can slip on steep snowfields.

82319.q: How does old snow on a snowfield often feel in spring?
82319.e: Old snow thaws during the day and freezes again at night. This makes it grainy and wet.

82320.q: What can form from snowfields over many years?
82320.e: If snow stays every year, it gets pressed into ice under its own weight. This is how a glacier can form.
82320.m: Snow that stays can turn into a glacier.

82321.q: What protects your eyes on a bright snowfield?
82321.e: It is very glaring on a snowfield. Good sunglasses protect your eyes from the strong light.

82322.q: What does the meltwater from snowfields do in summer?
82322.e: In summer the snow melts slowly. The water flows into streams, rivers and lakes.
82322.m: Meltwater fills the streams in summer.

82323.q: Why do you get sunburnt quickly on snowfields?
82323.e: The bright snow strongly reflects the sunlight. That is why almost twice as much light hits your skin, and you need sun cream.
82323.m: On snow you need sun cream.

a: A deep shaft in the glacier ice
82324.e: A glacier mill is a round, deep shaft in the ice of a glacier. Meltwater swirls down it into the depths.
82324.m: A glacier mill is a shaft in the glacier ice.

82325.q: What grinds a round hole into the rock at the bottom of a glacier mill?
a: Swirling water with sand and stones
82325.e: The water plunges through the glacier mill right down to the rock. There it swirls sand and gravel round and round and so grinds out a round hole.
82325.m: Swirling water with sand and stones grinds round holes into the rock.

82326.q: Why is a glacier mill called a “mill”?
a: The water turns and grinds inside it
Flour used to be ground there
It has sails like a windmill
82326.e: In a glacier mill, the water swirls round and grinds sand and stones. That is like a mill.
82326.m: In a glacier mill, the water turns like in a mill.

82327.q: What often lies right at the bottom of a glacier pothole?
82327.e: The stones were turned round and round by the water for a long time. This ground them round and smooth.
82327.m: Round, smooth stones often lie in glacier potholes.

82328.q: What shape are the walls of a glacier mill?
82328.e: The swirling water melts and grinds the walls round and round. That is why they are round and smooth.
82328.m: Glacier mills have round, smooth walls.

82329.q: Why do you find round holes from glacier mills even where there is no glacier today?
a: There used to be a glacier there
82329.e: In the Ice Age there were glaciers in many places in Switzerland. When they melted, the round holes were left in the rock.
82329.m: Round holes in the rock show that there used to be a glacier there.

82330.q: Where does the water plunge to in a glacier mill?
a: Down to the rock bed under the glacier
82330.e: The meltwater flows over the ice into the glacier mill. Then it plunges down to the rock bed under the glacier.
82330.m: The water of a glacier mill plunges down to the rock bed.

82331.q: How long did the water take to grind a deep hole into the rock under a glacier mill?
82331.e: Rock is very hard. The water with sand and stones had to swirl round for a very long time before a deep hole formed.
82331.m: Deep holes in the rock took a long time to form.

82332.q: Which city is the well-known Glacier Garden in?
82332.e: The Glacier Garden is in Lucerne. There you can see traces of the Ice Age right in the middle of the city.
82332.m: The Glacier Garden is in Lucerne.

82333.q: What can you see in the rock at the Glacier Garden in Lucerne?
82333.e: In the Glacier Garden you can see big, round holes in the rock. These glacier potholes were drilled by the water of a glacier.
82333.m: You can see glacier potholes at the Glacier Garden in Lucerne.

82335.q: What was someone trying to build when the Glacier Garden was discovered?
82335.e: Josef Wilhelm Amrein-Troller wanted to dig a wine cellar. While digging, the glacier potholes came to light.
82335.m: The Glacier Garden was found while building a wine cellar.

82336.q: What can you get lost in at the Glacier Garden in Lucerne?
82336.e: At the Glacier Garden there is a maze with lots of mirrors. It is easy to get lost in it.
82336.m: There is a mirror maze at the Glacier Garden.

82337.q: Which famous monument with an animal is right next to the Glacier Garden?
82337.e: The Lion Monument is a dying lion carved into the rock. It is only a few steps away from the Glacier Garden.
82337.m: The Lion Monument is next to the Glacier Garden.

82338.q: What time do the glacier potholes in the Glacier Garden in Lucerne come from?
82338.e: The holes formed about 20,000 years ago. At that time it was much colder than today.
82338.m: The glacier potholes in Lucerne come from the Ice Age.

82339.q: What lay over today's city of Lucerne in the Ice Age?
82339.e: In the Ice Age the glaciers reached far into the Central Plateau. There was thick ice over Lucerne too.
82339.m: In the Ice Age there was a glacier over Lucerne.

82340.q: In which Swiss city do two big erratic boulders, the Pierres du Niton, stick out of the lake?
82340.e: The two Pierres du Niton lie in the harbour of Geneva in Lake Geneva. A glacier carried them there from the Mont Blanc area in the Ice Age.
82340.m: The Pierres du Niton are in Geneva.

82341.q: Why is an erratic boulder called a “Findling” (foundling) in German?
a: It lies there out of place, as if found
82341.e: An erratic boulder is often made of a different rock from its surroundings. It lies there as if someone had put it down.
82341.m: An erratic boulder does not match the rock around it.

82342.q: Where in Switzerland can you find lots of erratic boulders?
82342.e: In the Ice Age the glaciers reached far into the Central Plateau. That is why there are lots of erratic boulders there.
82342.m: There are lots of erratic boulders on the Central Plateau.

82343.q: What can experts tell from erratic boulders?
a: How far glaciers used to reach
82343.e: Glaciers carried the boulders to their edges. That is why erratic boulders show how far the ice used to reach.
82343.m: Erratic boulders show how far the glaciers used to reach.

82344.q: How big can erratic boulders be?
a: Only as big as a pea
Only as big as an egg
Only as big as an apple
82344.e: Some erratic boulders are huge and weigh many tonnes. Some are as big as a house.
82344.m: Some erratic boulders are as big as a house.
